Title: Questions that came up at the last tournament....

Messages.Author: Henrik Isaksson
Messages.Body:
1. Is it ever legal to agree to a withdraw-deal if it gives one player a
gamewin?
Ex. 5 player table. One player is ousted. There are almost no time left, and
none of the players have any chance of ousting anyone. Are the players
without VP allowed to agree to a deal that everyone (but one) withdraws,
leaving the table with a 2-1-1-1-0 VP split. The way I see it, all the
players are maximizing their VP's (they are all getting 0,5 VP more) but
they are allso giving away a GW...

2. Are you allowed to keep a deal that you have made, even if it ends up
with you not getting a GW?
Ex. 5 player table. A-B-C-D-E. C makes a deal with A that if A helps him, C
will give A 2 VP. C then ousts B, and D ousts E. C now cannot give A 2VP and
himself getting a gamewin. Are he allowed to aid in ousting D and then
withdrawing (even though he'd at that point easily could have taken the
remaining VPs)?

3. What happens in this scenario: 2 players are left in a game, with 1 VP
each. The time is almost out and it lookes like they'll time-out, giving
them 1,5 VP each. A bystander (another player, or someone not involved in
the tournament) says: Why don't you let one of you withdraw? The players now
want to withdraw before the time is out.

4. Just to be really sure once again: When are you allowed to accept a deal
that gives you more VP, but gives someone else a gamewin? The way I
understand it is that if you're without any chance of getting any more VP's,
you can make a deal that, for instance, gives you 1 VP and another player 4
VP. But exactly how little must the chance be to get a GW for you to be
allowed to make the deal. I mean, there's always a theoretical chance that
you could win. Should it be less than 1% or something like that? The same
question applies to when you're allowed to oust yourself... Let's say you
have no minions, 6 pool left and only vampires with 6+ capacity in the
crypt. Theoretically you could get pool from someone's parity shift or see
you prey get ousted by a KRC, even if the chance is very slim. Exactly when
are you allowed to, for instance, transfer yourself out?

I'd apreciate some *good* answers on these questions, especially number 4,
preferably with confirmation by LSJ, because questions like these allways
seem to come up at the tournaments, and noone has the truth...

/Henrik Isaksson, prince of Halmstad, Sweden

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <af7dra$bug2j$1...@ID-135400.news.dfncis.de>, Henrik Isaksson

<hen...@nissamedia.net> writes:
>1. Is it ever legal to agree to a withdraw-deal if it gives one player a
>gamewin?

If you could not get a gamewin (in the opinion of the judge or whoever),
then you are legally entitled to maximise your VPs too.

>2. Are you allowed to keep a deal that you have made, even if it ends up
>with you not getting a GW?

Yes.

When you make a deal, you are required to make a deal that obeys the
rules but you can follow through with a deal even if it's not
necessarily in your best interests when it comes to it.

If you always had to back-stab when you made a deal, no-one could ever
make any deal.

>Ex. 5 player table. A-B-C-D-E. C makes a deal with A that if A helps him, C
>will give A 2 VP.

If the deal is "A chooses to give up the chance of a game win for two
victory points", you'd need someone to check that that was a legitimate
deal for A.

If a deal is made that says "I will not get a game win", get someone to
check that that's in that person's interests.

>C then ousts B, and D ousts E. C now cannot give A 2VP and
>himself getting a gamewin. Are he allowed to aid in ousting D and then
>withdrawing (even though he'd at that point easily could have taken the
>remaining VPs)?

Assuming that the deal was legal in the first place, going along with it
in the end is legal.

Breaking it is also legal.

>3. What happens in this scenario: 2 players are left in a game, with 1 VP
>each. The time is almost out and it lookes like they'll time-out, giving
>them 1,5 VP each. A bystander (another player, or someone not involved in
>the tournament) says: Why don't you let one of you withdraw? The players now
>want to withdraw before the time is out.

The judge would be obliged to fix the introduction of outside
assistance. (Receiving such is a form of cheating, under 5.1, but there
is nothing you can do about random people just shouting things out.)

If, in the judge's opinion, neither player was about to suggest such
just before the time-out, I would be inclined to rule (as a judge) that
both players received .5 VP, assuming that it had timed out.

>4. Just to be really sure once again: When are you allowed to accept a deal
>that gives you more VP, but gives someone else a gamewin?

When you could not gain a game win.

>The way I
>understand it is that if you're without any chance of getting any more VP's,
>you can make a deal that, for instance, gives you 1 VP and another player 4
>VP. But exactly how little must the chance be to get a GW for you to be
>allowed to make the deal.

Things aren't exact.

>I mean, there's always a theoretical chance that
>you could win. Should it be less than 1% or something like that?

Erm, quite how are you planning to mathematically determine a 1% chance?

--
James Coupe

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On Mon, 24 Jun 2002 17:29:55 +0200, Henrik Isaksson wrote:

>1. Is it ever legal to agree to a withdraw-deal if it gives one player a
>gamewin?

It's stupid that VEKN rules encourage players to withdraw rather then
fight it out until the end. (because withdrawal is worth 1 VP while
survival is only worth 0.5 VP) If survival wasn't penalised then this
question wouldn't arise.

>2. Are you allowed to keep a deal that you have made, even if it ends up
>with you not getting a GW?

LSJ will say yes but I'll still call such action cheating.

>3. What happens in this scenario: 2 players are left in a game, with 1 VP
>each. The time is almost out and it lookes like they'll time-out, giving
>them 1,5 VP each. A bystander (another player, or someone not involved in
>the tournament) says: Why don't you let one of you withdraw? The players now
>want to withdraw before the time is out.

That's the perverse VEKN incentive for withdrawal again.

>4. Just to be really sure once again: When are you allowed to accept a deal
>that gives you more VP, but gives someone else a game win?

In practise, the answer seems to be any time you feel like it. Has
doing this ever been forbidden or penalised?

With the example of the World Cup fresh in our minds, one might see
whether the game could provide some equivalent of the penalty shootout
to resolve a game which didn't produce a natural winner. Doomtown has
something of the sort - a final shootout between players that have
equal tie-break points. I can't think of an appropriate equivalent in
VTES but maybe you can ...?

Andrew

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
"Andrew S. Davidson" wrote:
> On Mon, 24 Jun 2002 17:29:55 +0200, Henrik Isaksson wrote:
> >4. Just to be really sure once again: When are you allowed to accept a deal
> >that gives you more VP, but gives someone else a game win?
>
> In practise, the answer seems to be any time you feel like it. Has
> doing this ever been forbidden or penalised?

Playing to achieve the best finish you can has only ever been penalized
by the old tournament rules that didn't rank game wins over total VPs,
and then only in a small portion of the cases.

The current rules no longer penealize playing for best possible finish
in game even in those small portion of cases.

Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
"Andrew S. Davidson" <a...@csi.com> wrote in message
news:11A7CBE76E8DC82B.E2EAC57A...@lp.airnews.net...

> On Mon, 24 Jun 2002 17:29:55 +0200, Henrik Isaksson wrote:
>
> >1. Is it ever legal to agree to a withdraw-deal if it gives one player a
> >gamewin?
>
> It's stupid that VEKN rules encourage players to withdraw rather then
> fight it out until the end. (because withdrawal is worth 1 VP while
> survival is only worth 0.5 VP) If survival wasn't penalised then this
> question wouldn't arise.

Survival isn't penalized, it's pointless. You have done nothing
worth rewarding by making a game go to time. Withdrawing is
quite difficult if you're not being allowed to do it by your
opponents; if a game is stalemated, then yes, it's to the
advantage of all players still in it to agree to discard through
their decks as fast as they can and then withdraw instead of
continuing to play within the stalemate until time runs out.
But why is this a problem? It only applies to games where *no
one* sees a chance of accomplishing anything before time runs
out.

> >2. Are you allowed to keep a deal that you have made, even if it ends up
> >with you not getting a GW?
>
> LSJ will say yes but I'll still call such action cheating.

You're allowed to break it, too... and IMO if you're smart,
you will. And you're only allowed to keep such a deal if it
was legal in the first place; IMO you can rarely (legally)
offer a deal where you help someone else win a game.

> >3. What happens in this scenario: 2 players are left in a game, with 1 VP
> >each. The time is almost out and it lookes like they'll time-out, giving
> >them 1,5 VP each. A bystander (another player, or someone not involved in
> >the tournament) says: Why don't you let one of you withdraw? The players
now
> >want to withdraw before the time is out.
>
> That's the perverse VEKN incentive for withdrawal again.

Not really perverse. It's better to withdraw than to go to
time, but it's better to get a VP and then go to time than
to withdraw. In other words, if you can manage to work
toward the goal of the game, it's better to not withdraw.

> >4. Just to be really sure once again: When are you allowed to accept a
deal
> >that gives you more VP, but gives someone else a game win?
>
> In practise, the answer seems to be any time you feel like it. Has
> doing this ever been forbidden or penalised?

People throwing games will always be penalized/forbidden in
tournaments I'm judging. I'm sure most judges feel the same
way. People accepting deals that let others win a game, when
they have no chance of winning themselves, is probably an
unavoidable feature of multiplayer one-winner games.

> With the example of the World Cup fresh in our minds, one might see
> whether the game could provide some equivalent of the penalty shootout
> to resolve a game which didn't produce a natural winner. Doomtown has
> something of the sort - a final shootout between players that have
> equal tie-break points. I can't think of an appropriate equivalent in
> VTES but maybe you can ...?

You could do something like this, but I don't know how you'd
do it while keeping the incentive to finish games before time
instead of relying on the "shootout".

Josh

Messages.Body:
"James Coupe" <ja...@zephyr.org.uk> wrote in message
news:axGmR6jv...@gratiano.zephyr.org.uk...

> In message <af7dra$bug2j$1...@ID-135400.news.dfncis.de>, Henrik Isaksson
> <hen...@nissamedia.net> writes:
> >1. Is it ever legal to agree to a withdraw-deal if it gives one player a
> >gamewin?
>
> If you could not get a gamewin (in the opinion of the judge or whoever),
> then you are legally entitled to maximise your VPs too.

Sure. You might not *want* to, though, if you're more concerned
about the "other guy" getting a GW than about you getting an
extra 0.5 VP.

> >2. Are you allowed to keep a deal that you have made, even if it ends up
> >with you not getting a GW?
>
> Yes.
>
> When you make a deal, you are required to make a deal that obeys the
> rules but you can follow through with a deal even if it's not
> necessarily in your best interests when it comes to it.
>
> If you always had to back-stab when you made a deal, no-one could ever
> make any deal.

That last isn't entirely true. Some deals have no "downside"
when it comes time to keep them. For example you make a deal
with your grandpredator that she will diablerize one of your
predator's vampires, and you'll vote to save in the bloodhunt.
It's in your interest to keep your deal, if you believe she
won't be able to put enough pressure on your predator without
that vampire.

It's true that it would greatly reduce the number of possible
deals if it *were* illegal to keep deals that would be
advantageous to break, though.

> >3. What happens in this scenario: 2 players are left in a game, with 1 VP
> >each. The time is almost out and it lookes like they'll time-out, giving
> >them 1,5 VP each. A bystander (another player, or someone not involved in
> >the tournament) says: Why don't you let one of you withdraw? The players
now
> >want to withdraw before the time is out.
>
> The judge would be obliged to fix the introduction of outside
> assistance. (Receiving such is a form of cheating, under 5.1, but there
> is nothing you can do about random people just shouting things out.)
>
> If, in the judge's opinion, neither player was about to suggest such
> just before the time-out, I would be inclined to rule (as a judge) that
> both players received .5 VP, assuming that it had timed out.

But note that there's no such thing as "agree to withdraw, you
all automatically withdraw" in the VEKN rules. All the players
have to actually burn through their entire libraries and fulfill
the withdrawal conditions in the rulebook. In other words, it's
not always feasible to do an "agree to withdraw" deal if people
*have* been trying to oust each other until nearly the time
limit.

Sort of a tangent there, I guess. :-)

Josh

Something I've observed that's related but doen't answer your questions.
I've found deal making to be a lot more difficult under the GW system.
No-one wants to give you a GW and you don't want to give anyone else a GW,
this makes it very difficult to make VP deals. In 5 player games 2-2-1
splits used to happen reasonably often as most ppl were happy to get 2 VPs a
round because doing so usually got you into the final. Under the GW system
2-2-1 splits are undesireable, usually because both of the ppl who would
normally be happy with 2 VPs want to try to get that 3rd one and the GW.
Personally I think this is a good thing. How has the GW rule affected ppls
deal making in other tournaments?

Now for a bit of a rant-ish thing. This whole maximising your VPs thing is a
bit of a joke. I mean, it's all very subjective. To me, you should never be
allowed to transfer yourself out, that's not maximising your VPs. You never
know, someone might plan on Life Booning you and keeping you alive so that
they can get that VP. Only to find themselves ousted and you're able to get
a VP. I frequently go to lengths to keep my "cross table buddies" in the
game. Someone might call an Ancient Influence, giving you 5 pool, loosing
your prey 2 and giving you a chance to get a VP. It's not likely but you
just never know, which is why I always fight to the bitter end.

It seems to me though that, despite having this maximising your VPs rule,
you can pretty-much do whatever the hell you want, all you have to do is
claim that your situation was hopeless or that you thought you'd be
maximising your VPs or that you just made some poor decisions. It just seems
a rather pointless and unenforceable rule the way it is being interpereted.

Messages.Author: Curevei
Messages.Body:
>Something I've observed that's related but doen't answer your questions.
>I've found deal making to be a lot more difficult under the GW system.
>No-one wants to give you a GW and you don't want to give anyone else a GW,
>this makes it very difficult to make VP deals. In 5 player games 2-2-1
>splits used to happen reasonably often as most ppl were happy to get 2 VPs a
>round because doing so usually got you into the final. Under the GW system
>2-2-1 splits are undesireable, usually because both of the ppl who would
>normally be happy with 2 VPs want to try to get that 3rd one and the GW.
>Personally I think this is a good thing. How has the GW rule affected ppls
>deal making in other tournaments?

My deal making? I delay deals that involve someone winning a table by a round.
Once you get past the first round, I see the same level of tournament
manipulation that existed prior (for "local-sized" tournaments, big tournaments
will always be different). So, I don't believe the TW system solved the
problem of playing to the tournament rather than to individual games. Might
have made it better, might not; there's a bunch of hidden effects.

Also, how one plays depends upon how the prizes are doled out. We had one
tournament where each table was worth X boosters. If someone won the table,
they got the boosters. If no one did, those boosters were opened and randomly
given out to all of the participants at the end of the tournament. The winner
got whatever prizes were set aside for the final table. IOW, getting to the
final table by itself didn't get you squat. I believe something like this
system is a good way to encourage people to focus on their games rather than
play to the tournament. But, like anything that heavily rewards winning
tables, does lead to an all or nothing experience.

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On Mon, 24 Jun 2002 14:57:37 -0400, Joshua Duffin wrote:

>advantage of all players still in it to agree to discard through
>their decks as fast as they can and then withdraw instead of
>continuing to play within the stalemate until time runs out.
>But why is this a problem?

Because it makes a mockery of the game. Instead of playing hard to
try to squeeze one last oust in, the players start playing a real-time
card-burning exercise that's more like Twitch, Brawl or Falling. The
game was not designed to played in this way and the tournament rules
shouldn't encourage it.

>It only applies to games where *no one* sees a chance of accomplishing
>anything before time runs out.

I've not done this but imagine that there is huge peer pressure to
cooperate to beat the system. What if one player wants to stop and
re-evaluate the situation, part-way through this play-acting? The
players should be doing this at every step but I expect that the
others would come down hard on anyone who tried to do so.

>People accepting deals that let others win a game, when
>they have no chance of winning themselves, is probably an
>unavoidable feature of multiplayer one-winner games.

I've run and played in 100+ multi-player tournaments for Shadowfist
and have _never_ seen it happen in that game. The deal-making that
you get in VTES is extreme - I've not seen anything like it since I
played Diplomacy a lot and, in that game, the deal-making came with a
healthy expectation that deals would be broken. That's why I rail
against VTES deal-making practises - they are way out of line with
what I expect to see in a multi-player game.

>You could do something like this, but I don't know how you'd
>do it while keeping the incentive to finish games before time
>instead of relying on the "shootout".

What incentive? The current incentive is to switch to mutual
withdrawal when time runs out.

Here's an alternative idea which would keep players fighting hard to
the end. If the game times out and there is no proper winner then the
table win would be divided amongst the survivors in proportion to
their VP with the edge counting as a VP for this purpose. Example:

3 survivors with 1 VP, 1 VP and 0 VP. The first player has the edge.
He gets 2/3 of a table win and the second player gets 1/3. The player
with nothing gets nothing.

Now you can fiddle with the scoring for this but the general idea is
to encourage a scramble for the edge which would make the end-game
bear a better resemblance to the normal play of the game than mutual
withdrawal does.

Andrew

"Andrew S. Davidson" <a...@csi.com> wrote in message

> On Mon, 24 Jun 2002 14:57:37 -0400, Joshua Duffin wrote:

> try to squeeze one last oust in, the players start playing a real-time

> game was not designed to played in this way and the tournament rules

I don't really think they do encourage it. This only happens,
in my experience, when no one believes they have any chance
of squeezing that last oust in; if they *did*, they'd benefit
hugely from trying for it rather than agreeing to a withdrawal
attempt.

> >It only applies to games where *no one* sees a chance of accomplishing
> >anything before time runs out.
>
> I've not done this but imagine that there is huge peer pressure to
> cooperate to beat the system. What if one player wants to stop and
> re-evaluate the situation, part-way through this play-acting? The
> players should be doing this at every step but I expect that the
> others would come down hard on anyone who tried to do so.

I haven't seen such peer pressure. I agree that players
should be able to stop partway through and don't think the
others would have any realistic way to "come down hard" on
them. Have you actually seen these "withdrawal pacts" become
a "problem" in tournament play? From my experience you're
suggesting a solution to a problem that doesn't exist.

> >People accepting deals that let others win a game, when
> >they have no chance of winning themselves, is probably an
> >unavoidable feature of multiplayer one-winner games.
>
> I've run and played in 100+ multi-player tournaments for Shadowfist
> and have _never_ seen it happen in that game.

Neither have I, but (while admitting that I haven't played
Shadowfist tournaments regularly for a couple years now)
I suspect this is because Shadowfist players have yet to
figure out and play to the tiebreakers. And probably also
because "getting second" in Shadowfist isn't rewarded (at
least under the systems I was familiar with) nearly as much
as it is in VTES, and because it's much less worthwhile in
Fist to help someone else into second place in return for
them helping you win - in Fist winning requires a lot less
set up than VTES. (in VTES you have to defeat at least two
players sequentially to win while being attacked constantly
by a third; in Fist you have to defeat three, but all at
once and only for an instant.)

> The deal-making that
> you get in VTES is extreme - I've not seen anything like it since I
> played Diplomacy a lot and, in that game, the deal-making came with a
> healthy expectation that deals would be broken. That's why I rail
> against VTES deal-making practises - they are way out of line with
> what I expect to see in a multi-player game.

I feel that the deal-making in VTES should also come with a
healthy expectation that deals will be broken, but there
does seem to be some dissension on this point. :-)

> >You could do something like this, but I don't know how you'd
> >do it while keeping the incentive to finish games before time
> >instead of relying on the "shootout".
>
> What incentive? The current incentive is to switch to mutual
> withdrawal when time runs out.

The incentive now is to finish games rather than let them
go to time, because if a game goes to time VPs are lost (with
"living" players being worth only 0.5 VP where they'd be
worth 1 VP dead). If there were a shootout system that assigned
all VPs/GWs, there would be less incentive to try to finish
the game before time; you could try to stall until the end and
win the shootout instead.

Mutual withdrawal at nearly-time is still inferior to finishing
legitimately; people will probably not agree to a withdrawal
pact that gives someone a game win, and if no one is getting a
game win it would've been much better to finish legitimately.

> Here's an alternative idea which would keep players fighting hard to
> the end. If the game times out and there is no proper winner then the
> table win would be divided amongst the survivors in proportion to
> their VP with the edge counting as a VP for this purpose. Example:
>
> 3 survivors with 1 VP, 1 VP and 0 VP. The first player has the edge.
> He gets 2/3 of a table win and the second player gets 1/3. The player
> with nothing gets nothing.
>
> Now you can fiddle with the scoring for this but the general idea is
> to encourage a scramble for the edge which would make the end-game
> bear a better resemblance to the normal play of the game than mutual
> withdrawal does.

This was suggested several times right after the GW system
was implemented; as written it entirely undermines the point
of the GW system. If you don't have to actually *win* a
game to get (at least part of) a game win, then dealmaking
for "split wins" becomes more attractive again.

Giving a "bonus" for the Edge is interesting but could also
encourage "slow play" toward the end of the game with each
player trying to spend as long as possible on her own turn
where she's holding the Edge. And of course the opponents
would try to slow down any attempts to get the Edge from
them...

Josh

manipulating the preliminary rounds". I'm more used to
just seeing everyone try to manipulate every game toward
their own victory, when possible; when not possible there's
the occasional spitefulness on the way out but I don't
recall noticing any serious "fixing" attempts. Maybe it's
a regional variation thing?

> Also, how one plays depends upon how the prizes are doled out. We had one
> tournament where each table was worth X boosters. If someone won the
table,
> they got the boosters.

I like this approach a lot and have been using it for the
last few sanctioned tournaments here - X has only equaled
1 so far, and there have been additional prizes for 2nd
through 5th finalists, but I like the additional incentive
to "play to the game".

> I believe something like this system is a good way to
> encourage people to focus on their games rather than
> play to the tournament. But, like anything that heavily
> rewards winning tables, does lead to an all or nothing
> experience.

As far as prizing goes, I've been also having a "one pack
for showing up" "prize" (essentially the same as a "one
pack entry fee") so that no one goes home with nothing. But
there's not nearly enough prize support (without charging
quite a bit for entry fees) to give, for example, a pack per
VP in prelim rounds. It'd certainly be nice, though. And
could be done with a "one pack per round" entry fee, but I
don't know if people really want to "spend" that much on
regular VTES tournaments.

Josh

Messages.Author: Curevei
Messages.Body:
>> >Personally I think this is a good thing. How has the GW rule affected
>ppls
>> >deal making in other tournaments?
>>
>> My deal making? I delay deals that involve someone winning a
>> table by a round.
>
>Doesn't this only apply if you have yourself won the first round,
>though? I'd think you couldn't afford to "give away" game wins
>without having at least one yourself.

Actual example: My grandprey from round one became my predator round two. He
was almost a lock for the finals. A three VP TW would have probably had gotten
me in. So, from the beginning of the second round, my interest was a 3-2
split. He didn't particularly want me in the finals [another aspect of
manipulation], but as I had a deck that could wreck him, it wasn't a horrible
idea to go for the split to guarantee that he'd get in or to get a better
seeding.

Yes, if no one has a TW and it appears that a TW is absolutely necessary, then
it's hard to deal. But, as soon as anyone in your game does, there's all sorts
of potential for manipulation.

>Personally I'd not even be comfortable "giving away" game wins
>after having one, both due to the "play to win" rule and the
>fact that many tournaments I play in have enough players that
>one GW isn't necessarily enough to get you into the finals.
>It's a different story when you don't see any chance for getting
>the game win yourself, I suppose.

Of course, it depends on what the projected cut line is. Whether the
tournament has two prelims or three and how many tables there are will affect
this going in. With three prelims and a bunch of tables, there's not a whole
lot you can do, but then, there never was.

Given how many of our games time out, one TW in a two prelim tournament is
nearly a lock, while one TW and 5+ VPs is pretty much a lock for a three
prelim.

Another example: Second to last tournament, I somehow ended up with a TW after
the first round. Three prelim, so I had a bit more work to do for the
guaranteed slot. I went into my second round with a 1-2 VP goal. I was
willing to split 2-2-1 with my grandpredator, but he waffled to where I was
forced to get another TW.

>> Once you get past the first round, I see the same level of tournament
>> manipulation that existed prior (for "local-sized" tournaments, big
>tournaments
>> will always be different).
>
>I've never really seen that much manipulation in the sense
>of, say, "trying to control who gets to the finals by
>manipulating the preliminary rounds". I'm more used to
>just seeing everyone try to manipulate every game toward
>their own victory, when possible; when not possible there's
>the occasional spitefulness on the way out but I don't
>recall noticing any serious "fixing" attempts. Maybe it's
>a regional variation thing?

In the third round of that tournament, having 2 TWs in hand, my interest was
entirely in manipulating the final. I didn't want anyone from my table in
except the person already in, so I did as little as possible. The irony was
that I still ended up with more VPs than anyone else when the game timed out.
But, if I had to do something for myself or if I particularly wanted someone
else in the finals from my table, the game would have been entirely different.
I might even have had an interest in trying to set my predator up for a sweep
if I particularly wanted him in the finals for match up purposes.

Maybe it's just being used to playing multiplayer CCG tournaments with final
tables, but I see a lot of potential for playing to the tournament over playing
to the individual games even in the postTW era. Note that I don't think is
necessarily bad, it's just the nature of multiround CCG tournaments.

Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
"Curevei" <cur...@aol.commetal> wrote in message

news:20020625183749...@mb-fz.aol.com...

> Actual example: My grandprey from round one became my predator round two.
He
> was almost a lock for the finals. A three VP TW would have probably had
gotten
> me in. So, from the beginning of the second round, my interest was a 3-2
> split. He didn't particularly want me in the finals [another aspect of
> manipulation], but as I had a deck that could wreck him, it wasn't a
horrible
> idea to go for the split to guarantee that he'd get in or to get a better
> seeding.

You figured a 3-2 split with you getting 3 was good enough? By
the "play to win" rule he's not allowed to take that deal unless
he has no chance of getting more than 2 VPs, though. Admittedly
it's hard to prove either way but as a judge Iwould rarely allow
anyone to accept a game-losing deal. A prey's deck that "wrecks"
you isn't enough justification (IMO) to take a losing deal.

> Yes, if no one has a TW and it appears that a TW is absolutely
> necessary, then it's hard to deal. But, as soon as anyone in your
> game does, there's all sorts of potential for manipulation.

As long as people aren't too concerned with the "play to win"
rule. A difficult rule to enforce, of course.

> Of course, it depends on what the projected cut line is. Whether
> the tournament has two prelims or three and how many tables there
> are will affect this going in. With three prelims and a bunch of
> tables, there's not a whole lot you can do, but then, there never
> was.

True. So maybe big tournaments are the way to go? :-)

> Another example: Second to last tournament, I somehow ended up with
> a TW after the first round. Three prelim, so I had a bit more work to
> do for the guaranteed slot. I went into my second round with a 1-2 VP
> goal. I was willing to split 2-2-1 with my grandpredator, but he
> waffled to where I was forced to get another TW.

Heh. It is a hardship. What does this illustrate, though?
That "gaming the tournament" is desirable to the players? Not
entirely surprising I guess, but it is at least to some extent
prohibited by the letter and spirit of the tournament rules. If
the players don't care about that (and I don't mean to make any
moral judgements here) those rules may not be very enforceable,
though.

> In the third round of that tournament, having 2 TWs in hand, my
> interest was entirely in manipulating the final.

OK.

> I didn't want anyone from my table in except the person already in,
> so I did as little as possible. The irony was that I still ended up
> with more VPs than anyone else when the game timed out. But, if I
> had to do something for myself or if I particularly wanted someone
> else in the finals from my table, the game would have been entirely
> different. I might even have had an interest in trying to set my
> predator up for a sweep if I particularly wanted him in the finals
> for match up purposes.

Hmm. Funny, yeah. I wonder if this is an argument in favor of
not publicizing standings and asking players not to discuss them?
Also not enforceable but might cut down on this kind of manipulation,
if people are interested in reducing it.

> Maybe it's just being used to playing multiplayer CCG tournaments
> with final tables, but I see a lot of potential for playing to the
> tournament over playing to the individual games even in the postTW
> era. Note that I don't think is necessarily bad, it's just the
> nature of multiround CCG tournaments.

Sure. Probably no scoring system can eliminate the incentive to
"play to the tournament" rather than "the game". I do think the
GW system has better "play to the game" incentives than the VPs
system did, though. Prizing the prelim tables for game winners
may also "help". I don't know what more could be done beyond
asking players to stick to the spirit of the "play to win" rules.
Again, if it *is* desired to reduce "manipulation".

Josh
